preamble: Implosivization of the voiced palatal series: Old and Middle Indo-Aryan j becomes the palatal implosive [ʄ]. Sindhi and Saraiki turned Middle Indo-Aryan initial voiced stops (and voiced geminates) into implosives, a change Masica (1991) calls highly distinctive within New Indo-Aryan; j gave ʄ alongside b > ɓ, d > ɗ (Saraiki ᶑ) and g > ɠ. Wikipedia says the Saraiki implosives have on the whole the same origin as the Sindhi ones, from the older plain voiced stops. Turner's Comparative Dictionary writes the Sindhi and Jukes' Lahnda (Saraiki) implosive as j̄. The change is not exceptionless: Turner (5155) gives Sindhi jaru 'water' with plain j. The input is filed here as [dʒ], as in the atlas's other Middle Indo-Aryan j entries and as Wikipedia transcribes the Saraiki plain series, but it is also transcribed [ɟ] (the IPA Handbook's Sindhi letters) or [dʑ] (Wiktionary's Sanskrit). Swahili shows the same pair synchronically: written j (except after a nasal) is realized as [dʒ] or implosive [ʄ]. Wikipedia calls [ʄ] an allophone of /dʒ/, while Wiktionary transcribes the phoneme itself as /ʄ/, so the direction of the Swahili variation is not settled.

examples.note: Turner 5213: S. j̄āru m. 'net', j̄āro m. 'cobweb'.
Wikipedia gives ʄɪbbʰ; Turner 5228 has Lahnda (Jukes) j̄ibh.
Turner 5213: Lahnda (Jukes) j̄ālā 'cobweb'. It contrasts with /dʒala/ 'niche'.

languageExamples.context: Written j (not after a nasal) has an implosive allophone [ʄ]; prenasalized nj is always [ⁿdʒ]. Wikipedia's 'Voiced palatal implosive' table calls it free variation, but no source states the conditioning

examples.note: Wikipedia's article on the palatal implosive gives this example, in free variation with /dʒ/. Wiktionary transcribes it /ˈʄɑ.nɑ/.
Wiktionary transcribes it /ˈʄi.nɑ/, treating ʄ as the phoneme. The [dʒ] ~ [ʄ] variation is the general statement for Swahili j and is not recorded for this word individually.
Wiktionary transcribes it /ˈʄi.tʃɔ/. Same caveat as jina.
